title: Arrays
summary: Tables with consecutive integer keys starting at 1: ordered lists. Players in a queue, loot drops, waypoints — if order matters, it's an array.

syntax: table.remove(pets, 1)             -- remove at index, shifts the rest

details.heading: What makes it an 'array'
details.body: A table whose keys are exactly 1..n with no gaps. `#t` returns n only for such tables. `table.insert(t, v)` appends at `#t + 1`; `table.insert(t, i, v)` inserts at position i.

explanation.whatItIs: An array is an ordered list. You add things to the end, take them out by position, and walk them in order — first to last.
explanation.whyItExists: Order matters constantly: turn order, chat history, pathfinding waypoints, spawn lists.
whenToUse: Stacks (`insert`/`remove` at the end) and queues
Collecting results to process later: `table.concat`, batch updates
whenNotToUse: When you look things up by name, use a dictionary instead: `inventory["sword"]` beats scanning an array
When order doesn't matter and you need fast 'is this in here?' checks, use a set-style dictionary: `owned[petId] = true`
explanation.mentalModel:
```text
pets:   [1]="Cat"  [2]="Dog"  [3]="Dragon"

pets[2]      --> "Dog"
pets[#pets]  --> last item  ("Dragon")
#pets        --> 3
```
Think of numbered lockers in a row, starting at locker 1.
tips: `pets[#pets]` is the idiom for 'the last element'
To loop backwards while removing: `for i = #t, 1, -1 do`
`table.find(t, value)` returns the first index of a value (Luau addition)
`table.sort(t)` sorts in place; pass a comparator for custom order
commonMistakes: Using index 0 — `pets[0]` is nil; arrays start at 1
Removing while looping forward: indices shift and you skip items — loop backwards instead
Making holes (assigning t[5] when #t is 2) and trusting #t afterwards

examples.title: A simple queue
examples.code:
local queue = {}

table.insert(queue, "Alice")   -- join the back
table.insert(queue, "Bob")

local next = table.remove(queue, 1)   -- serve the front
print(next)        --> Alice
print(queue[1])    --> Bob
examples.whyItWorks: `table.insert(t, v)` appends; `table.remove(t, 1)` takes the front and shifts everyone forward.

examples.title: Removing safely while looping
examples.code:
local enemies = { "Goblin", "Slime", "Goblin", "Bat" }

-- WRONG: for i = 1, #enemies do ... table.remove(enemies, i) — skips items!
-- RIGHT: walk backwards
for i = #enemies, 1, -1 do
    if enemies[i] == "Goblin" then
        table.remove(enemies, i)
    end
end

print(table.concat(enemies, ", "))   --> Slime, Bat
